title: Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, 3rd Movement: Structure, Texture and Tonality for Your Exam
content_html:
Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, iii: Getting Under the Skin of the Finale

This lesson zooms in on the third movement — the Allegro finale — of J S Bach’s Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 in D major. You already know the outline of the whole concerto; now you need the fine detail examiners actually test: how the movement is built, how the instruments interact, what makes the rhythm feel the way it does, and how the harmony moves. Treat this as your ‘deep dive’ lesson — every paragraph gives you vocabulary and observations you can lift straight into an extended answer.

Where This Movement Sits: Recap of Context

Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 is a Baroque concerto grosso, composed by Bach around 1721 and dedicated to the Margrave of Brandenburg. A concerto grosso contrasts a small group of solo instruments, the concertino, with a larger body of strings, the ripieno. In this concerto the concertino is unusual: flute, violin and a harpsichord that is given a genuinely soloistic, virtuosic role rather than just accompanying — a landmark moment in keyboard writing. The famous extended harpsichord cadenza belongs to the first movement, so do not place it in the third movement by mistake in your exam answer; the finale instead gives the harpsichord continued prominence within fast, imitative dialogue rather than an unaccompanied solo passage.

Key fact: the third movement is a lively Allegro in 2/4 time with a gigue-like character. It is built from a single fugal subject that is worked through all three concertino instruments and the ripieno strings, giving the movement its unity and drive.

Structure: Fugal Opening, Contrasting Middle, Return

The movement opens with the violin stating a quick, dancing subject built from running quavers and semiquavers. This subject is then taken up in turn by flute and harpsichord in imitation, exactly as a fugue exposition works: each entry overlaps the previous one so the texture thickens as more parts enter. Once all the concertino voices have stated the subject, the ripieno strings join in, and the whole ensemble develops fragments of the idea through a series of episodes, moving briefly through related keys before the opening fugal idea returns.

Overall the finale behaves like a rounded, ternary-type design: an opening fugal idea (A), a contrasting central passage that explores new keys and lighter, thinner scoring (B), and a return of the opening material and key (a da-capo-style A) to close the movement satisfyingly in D major. Listen for how recognisable the opening subject is each time it reappears — that recurring ‘head-motif’ is your clearest structural signpost when following a score or a listening extract in the exam.

Key fact: examiners often ask you to identify where the opening fugal subject returns. Practise recognising its distinctive rising-then-falling quaver shape so you can spot it instantly, even played by a different instrument or in a different key.

Texture: Concertino, Ripieno and Imitation

The texture throughout is essentially contrapuntal, meaning several independent melodic lines interact rather than one clear melody sitting over accompanying chords. Imitative entries dominate: a musical idea introduced by one instrument is immediately imitated by another, usually at a different pitch, creating constant conversation between flute, violin and harpsichord. The continuo, provided by the harpsichord’s left hand together with cello and double bass, supports the harmony throughout, giving Baroque texture its characteristic firm bass line beneath the busy upper parts.

The concertino and ripieno groups are used for contrast of texture and volume rather than simply for contrast of melody. Passages for concertino alone feel light and transparent, three lines weaving together; when the ripieno strings enter, the texture thickens and the dynamic effect grows fuller, even though Baroque instruments cannot achieve gradual crescendos — this is terraced dynamics, sudden shifts in volume created by adding or removing groups of players rather than gradual dynamic shading.

Metre, Rhythm and Melody: The Gigue Feel

The movement is in 2/4, but the constant semiquaver and quaver movement gives it the light, bouncing, dance-like energy associated with a gigue, a lively Baroque dance often found closing a suite or concerto. This rhythmic drive is maintained almost without a break; there are very few long notes, and the sense of forward momentum is one of the most recognisable features of the whole finale.

Melodically, the fugal subject is built from scalic and arpeggio-based patterns typical of late Baroque instrumental writing — conjunct (stepwise) movement combined with small leaps that outline the underlying chord. Bach develops this material through sequence, repeating a short melodic pattern at successively higher or lower pitches, a device you should be ready to name when describing how the melodic material is extended across the movement.

Key fact: listen for decoration of the melodic line with trills and short scalic flourishes, especially in the flute and violin parts, and in virtuosic passagework for the harpsichord — this ornamentation is idiomatic of high Baroque style and worth naming specifically as ornamentation or decoration in your answers.

Harmony and Tonality: D major and its Related Keys

The movement is firmly rooted in D major, the tonic key of the whole concerto, giving the finale a bright, celebratory character appropriate to a closing movement. As is typical of Baroque instrumental music, the harmony moves through closely related keys during the central episodes — particularly the dominant, A major, and the relative minor, B minor — before a clear cadential return re-establishes D major for the final restatement of the fugal subject. This pattern of moving away from the tonic and decisively returning to it is a hallmark of Baroque tonal planning, and naming the specific keys involved (rather than simply saying ‘it modulates’) will earn you significantly more credit.

It is useful to compare this treatment of key with a very different concerto-era approach: Beethoven’s Piano Sonata No. 8 ‘Pathétique’, another set work from the same area of study, uses far more dramatic, unstable harmonic shifts and sudden dynamic contrasts befitting the Classical style, showing how tonality and key relationships were used differently by composers roughly seventy years apart.

Exam Skills: How Questions Target This Movement

Exam questions on this movement typically ask you to identify texture at a given point (is it imitative, contrapuntal, or does the ripieno reinforce a homophonic passage?), to name the key or describe a modulation, to spot where the fugal subject returns, or to identify instruments by their timbre, particularly distinguishing the harpsichord’s bright, plucked sound from the sustained tone of flute and violin. You may also be asked to comment on rhythmic character, where naming the gigue-like compound feel and continuous quaver/semiquaver movement scores well.

Always answer with specific musical vocabulary tied to a moment in the music rather than vague description: instead of writing ‘the instruments play together’, write ‘the flute and violin imitate the harpsichord’s fugal subject a bar apart, creating overlapping contrapuntal entries’. That level of precision, linked to structure, texture, tonality and rhythm together, is exactly what separates a top-band answer from a mid-band one.
exam_tip_html: When a question gives you a short extract and asks you to name the texture, do not just write ‘polyphonic’ and stop — examiners reward answers that identify which instruments are imitating which idea and roughly when (for example, ‘the violin imitates the flute’s entry of the fugal subject shortly after it is first heard’); a common mistake is naming the texture correctly but giving zero supporting evidence from the music, which caps the mark even if the terminology is right.
conclusion_html: You should now be able to talk confidently about the finale’s fugal structure, its concertino-versus-ripieno texture, its gigue-like rhythm and its D major tonal plan. Next, test yourself against short listening extracts from the movement, timing how quickly you can name the key, the texture and the instrument playing the subject at any given point.

practice_questions.text: Identify the metre of the third movement of Brandenburg Concerto No. 5.
practice_questions.marks: Award the mark for correctly stating 2/4.

practice_questions.text: Name the three instruments that make up the concertino group in this concerto.
practice_questions.marks: Award the mark for correctly naming flute, violin and harpsichord.

practice_questions.text: Describe the texture heard at the opening of the third movement.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for identifying imitative/contrapuntal texture and for noting the violin states the subject first, followed by imitative entries.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Bach creates a sense of structural return in the finale.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for reference to the fugal subject reappearing, the return to the tonic key of D major, and the overall ternary/da-capo-style shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain how key relationships contribute to the overall structure of the movement.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for identifying movement to related keys such as A major or B minor, description of departure from and return to D major, and linking this to the sense of resolution at the close.

practice_questions.text: Compare the role of the harpsichord in this movement with its role elsewhere in the concerto.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for noting the harpsichord's virtuosic cadenza occurs in the first movement, while in the finale it participates equally in imitative dialogue and continuo support rather than an unaccompanied solo.

glossary_terms.definition: A Baroque concerto form contrasting a small group of soloists with a larger ensemble.
The small group of solo instruments in a concerto grosso, here flute, violin and harpsichord.
The larger body of strings that accompanies and contrasts with the concertino.
The bass line and harmonic support, typically harpsichord plus cello and double bass, running through Baroque music.
A contrapuntal compositional technique where a subject is introduced and then imitated in turn by other parts.
When one musical part repeats a melodic idea shortly after another part has introduced it.
A three-part musical structure (A B A) where the opening material returns after a contrasting middle section.
The repetition of a melodic or rhythmic pattern at a higher or lower pitch.
A lively Baroque dance in compound or fast duple metre, often used to close a suite or concerto.
Sudden changes in volume created by adding or removing instrumental groups, typical of Baroque music.
The process of moving from one key to another within a piece of music.
Decorative notes such as trills or scalic flourishes added to a melodic line.

description: A close study of Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 finale covering its fugal structure, concertino-ripieno texture, gigue rhythm, melodic writing and D major tonality, with guidance on how these features are examined.
